title: hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna
hook: "where is he?" some ask. "he is not," some say. a hymn to Indra quotes its doubters out loud

segments.voice: Yesterday, hymns to Agni: the fire in the house, asked to be easy to approach, as a father to his son. Did you pause for a breath before you lit something? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-nine.
screen: `EASY TO REACH, AS A FATHER TO A SON.`

segments.voice: "Where is he?" people ask. "He isn't real," others answer. It could be an argument at a dinner table this week. It's a line from a hymn in the Rig Veda, book two, and the god being doubted is Indra, the storm, the warrior, the one who breaks the dam and lets the rivers run. The hymn could have left the doubters out. Instead it quotes them, right in the middle of the praise. Today: the second of four voices, Indra.
screen: `"WHERE IS HE?"` → `"HE ISN'T REAL."` → `A HYMN THAT QUOTES ITS DOUBTERS.`

segments.voice: Indra is the mighty one of the Rig Veda's storms. In its stories he fights Vritra, a serpent who has coiled around the waters and holds them back, and when Indra strikes him down, the rivers pour free. He drinks soma, rides with the storm, and stands with those who call on him. Book two, hymn twelve, is a hymn of praise to him, and it has a shape you can hear even in paraphrase. Verse after verse tells something Indra did: he steadied the shaking earth, he spread out the sky, he killed the serpent and set the rivers flowing. And verse after verse ends the same way. Sa janasa indrah. He, O people, is Indra. Then, in the fifth verse, the hymn turns. In paraphrase: the terrible one, about whom they ask, where is he? About whom they say, he is not. And the answer the singer gives isn't an argument. It's an invitation: put your trust in him. He, O people, is Indra. That's striking. A hymn of praise names, out loud, the people who don't believe in the god it's praising. It doesn't hide the question or pretend nobody asks it. It lets the question stand in the hymn, and answers it with trust, and goes on singing. Earlier on this path the Nasadiya Sukta asked who really knows how the world began. Here, a hymn to the god of the storm makes room for someone saying he isn't there at all.
screen: `INDRA FREES THE WATERS.` · `"HE, O PEOPLE, IS INDRA."` · `"WHERE IS HE?" "HE IS NOT."` · `THE QUESTION STAYS IN THE HYMN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let a question and a trust sit side by side. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you're unsure of: something about life, about faith, about a person, about yourself. Don't argue with it. Let it be asked. Then, next to it, find one thing you do trust, even something small: the floor holding you, the breath coming back, someone who has shown up for you. Hold both. When the mind tries to settle the question, let it stay a question. If you pray, you can offer both. The bell holds the time.
Hymns to Agni, and today, to Indra. In Rig Veda book two, hymn twelve, each verse ends, he, O people, is Indra, and one verse quotes those who say, he is not. Today's word.
Your line: hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna. Today, when someone voices a doubt, theirs or yours, let it be said out loud before anyone answers it. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Hymns to Indra are part of the Rig Veda's recitation, kept in Vedic schools; in later Hindu stories Indra appears as king of the gods and lord of rain.

original.note: Sanskrit: Indra, the Rig Veda's storm and warrior god, who frees the waters from Vritra.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hymn of praise only says good things about its god.
what it means: Rig Veda 2.12 praises Indra verse by verse, and in the middle names the people who say he doesn't exist.
what a scholar hears: the refrain sa janasa indrah closes the verses, and verse five quotes the doubters, utem ahur naisho astity enam, they say of him, he is not.

sources.ref: Rig Veda 2.12 (the refrain; verse 2 the earth steadied and the sky spread; verse 3 the serpent killed and the rivers freed; verse 5 the doubters and the call to trust)
Rig Veda 1.32 (Indra and Vritra; the waters released)
